newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 3.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- GERMAN BUSINESS LEADERS DOUBT 1999 START DATE

German business leaders have warned that few businesses are preparing for the start of a single European currency in January 1999, and have expressed concerns about whether the start date would be met at all. Speaking in a panel debate at the weekend, Ulrich Cartellieri, a Deutsche Bank board member, said there are fundamental doubts in both France and Germany about the whole concept. He also warned that Italy could not sustain a hard currency, and that "in the view of many, if Italy is admitted it could be a timebomb within the union".
-- UK CLOSE TO OPEN SKIES DEAL WITH US

The UK is reported to be closer to reaching a new "open skies" aviation accord with the US that would replace the 20- year old Bermuda II agreement. Although talks due to resume in Washington on Tuesday have been postponed due to illness, it is understood a more liberal accord is being sought because of the worldwide movement towards more openness in aviation, and in part to head off attempts by Brussels to negotiate on behalf of EU members. A US-UK open skies agreement is also a precondition set by the US before it will approve the planned British Airways merger with American Airlines.
-- SCOTTISH AMICABLE STICKS TO PLAN DESPITE BIDDING THREAT

Life insurance group Scottish Amicable, which last week rejected a takeover offer from Abbey National, has said it intends to proceed with attempts to gain policyholder support for its demutualisation plans. ScotAm hopes to shed its mutual status ahead of a 1 billion sterling to 1.5 billion stg floatation in three to five years. However, Abbey National is expected to come back with a renewed bid following the rejection of an offer valued at up to 1.4 billion stg.
-- EUROPE TURNS TO WTO ON US ANTI-CUBA LAW

The dispute between the European Union and the US over the Helms-Burton act, which authorises private US court cases against foreign companies "trafficking" in Cuban assets seized from Americans in the fifties, is set to test the World Trade Organisation. Brussels is expected this week to ask the WTO to name the members of its panel, which will rule on an EU complaint that Helms-Burton violates world trade rules. The US has threatened to block the case by vetoing the choice of panelists, and by challenging the WTO's right to judge the EU complaint.
-- EUROPEAN ACTION URGED TO CATCH UP ON TECHNOLOGY

A report prepared for the EU Council of Ministers warns that Europe's progress in closing the competitiveness gap with the US and Japan in information and communications technology is "slow or non-existent". The report calls for urgent political and economic action by all EU member countries, including a harmonization of telecommunications markets, acceleration of the reform of standardization procedures, and the merging of sector- specific research and development programmes to cover the entire industry spectrum.
-- NUMBERS COMPANY ATTEMPTS TO RING UP 1 MILLION STERLING

A north of England-based company, 21st Century Numbers, is asking 1 million stg for a pair of telephone numbers, as the market for distinctive or personalised numbers starts to take off in the UK. Observers suggest that the two numbers, 07000

MILLENNIUM and its mobile equivalent 0321 MILLENNIUM, will not reach the asking price, but the development demonstrates the confidence in the UK market following an explosion of growth in the business in the US. Oftel, the telecoms industry watchdog, has reserved one billion "personalised" numbers for the UK market.
-- CARMAKERS BLAMED FOR LOSS OF BUYERS' CONFIDENCE

A report from Cardiff Business School, specialists in the automotive industry, has claimed that car manufacturers and franchised dealers have themselves to blame for the loss of confidence among retail buyers in the new car market, and for plunging values in the used and "nearly new" sectors. The report points out that manufacturers are pouring more than 300,000 of their own "short cycle" cars -- maker and dealer company cars, courtesy cars, fleet and dealer demonstrators -- into the used car market each year.
-- US SURGE LIFTS WORLD DRUG SALES

An increase of 11 percent in US drug sales for the first 11 months of 1996 contributed to drug sales in the world's top ten markets exceeding $130 billion. The overall world sales figures for the period represent a 7 percent increase over the first 11 months of 1995. The figures, from market researchers IMS International, show that US drug sales topped $54 billion for the period. Japan, where the government introduced mandatory price cuts in early 1996, was the main drag on world growth, with an increase in sales of 2 percent, to $21.1 billion.
-- BUSINESS FAILS TO EXPLOIT 'INTRANET' SYSTEMS

A study carried out by Durlacher Multimedia in conjunction with UK-based marketing consultancy Romtec claims that British companies are lagging well behind their US counterparts in exploiting the potential of intranet systems. The study found that only 13 percent of the UK's top 1000 companies had installed intranets, compared to 63 percent in the US. It suggested that companies in the US are using intranets to develop fundamentally different ways of doing business, and, according to Edward Forwood, one of the authors, intranets "can show returns on investment of over 1000 percent".
